section.title: Shepherd the Flock
section.sectionRationale: As the letter closes, Peter turns to the care of the church under pressure: elders are to shepherd the flock humbly under the Chief Shepherd, the young are to submit, and all are to be clothed in humility, casting their cares on God and resisting the devil. It gathers the letter's themes of suffering, humility, and hope into a final charge and a great promise from the God of all grace.
section.thesis: Under the Chief Shepherd who will appear with an unfading crown, elders shepherd God's flock willingly and humbly, all clothe themselves in humility and cast their anxieties on the God who cares for them, and resisting the devil they trust that the God of all grace will Himself restore and establish them after a little suffering.
section.frameNote: Three movements: shepherd the flock under the Chief Shepherd, verses 1 to 4; humble yourselves and cast your cares on God, verses 5 to 7; and resist the devil, trusting the God of all grace, verses 8 to 11.

verses.text: As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you:
Be {{poimaino|shepherds}} of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not out of greed, but out of eagerness;
not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.
And when the {{archipoimen|Chief Shepherd}} appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.

Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with {{tapeinophrosyne|humility}} toward one another, because, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you.
Cast all your {{merimna|anxiety}} on Him, because He cares for you.

units.label: Resist the devil, trust the God of all grace
units.note: He will restore and establish you

verses.text: Be sober-minded and alert. Your {{antidikos|adversary}} the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.
Resist him, standing firm in your faith and in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering.

And after you have suffered for a little while, the {{theos_charitos|God of all grace}}, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself {{katartizo|restore}} you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you.
To Him be the power forever and ever. Amen.

poimaino.gloss: To shepherd, to tend a flock, including feeding, guiding, and guarding. Elders are to shepherd God's flock, not their own, caring for the people as a shepherd cares for sheep. The word echoes Jesus' charge to Peter, feed My sheep, and frames pastoral leadership as tender, watchful care rather than rule.

archipoimen.gloss: The Chief Shepherd, the head over all under-shepherds. Christ is the Chief Shepherd who owns the flock and will appear to reward faithful elders with an unfading crown of glory. Every human shepherd serves under Him and is accountable to Him, tending sheep that finally belong to Christ, not to themselves.

tapeinophrosyne.gloss: Humility, lowliness of mind. Peter tells all believers to clothe themselves with it toward one another, like tying on a servant's apron. Since God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, humility is the garment of those who live under God's mighty hand and expect Him, in time, to exalt them.

merimna.gloss: Anxiety, worry, the cares that weigh on the soul. Believers are to cast all their anxiety on God, throwing the whole burden onto Him. The ground is His personal care: He cares for you. Humility and casting cares belong together, for it is pride that insists on carrying its own burdens.

antidikos.gloss: An adversary, an opponent at law, an enemy. The devil is the believer's adversary, prowling like a roaring lion to devour. Yet he is to be resisted by standing firm in faith, not feared, for the God of all grace will soon restore His people. The enemy is real but already doomed under Christ's power.

theos_charitos.gloss: The God of all grace, the source of every kind of grace. Peter names God this way as he promises restoration after suffering. The God who has called His people to eternal glory in Christ is overflowing in grace, and it is His grace, not their strength, that will carry them through and bring them home.

katartizo.gloss: To restore, mend, or make complete, as one sets a broken bone or repairs a net. After a little suffering the God of all grace will Himself restore His people. The word promises that God does not merely rescue but mends what suffering has strained, making His people whole, firm, and fit for His eternal glory.

basic.context: Peter, himself an elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings, charges the church's elders: shepherd God's flock, not because you must or for money, but willingly and eagerly, not bossing people around but leading by example. When the Chief Shepherd, Jesus, appears, you will get a crown of glory that never fades. Younger believers should submit to the elders, and everyone should put on humility, because God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. So humble yourself under God's mighty hand, cast all your worries on Him, because He genuinely cares for you. Stay alert: the devil prowls like a lion. Resist him, standing firm in faith. And know this: after a little suffering, the God of all grace will Himself restore you and make you strong.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the letter's closing charge, and it ties together its main threads: suffering, humility, and hope. Leadership is defined as servant shepherding under Christ the Chief Shepherd, never as domineering. The promise of verse 10 is the letter's summit: after a little while of suffering, God Himself will restore, secure, strengthen, and establish His people. The suffering is real but brief; the glory is eternal.
basic.originalLanguages: Elders are to poimaino, shepherd, God's flock, awaiting the archipoimen, the Chief Shepherd. All are to put on tapeinophrosyne, humility, and cast their merimna, anxiety, on God who cares. The antidikos, the adversary, the devil, is to be resisted. The theos pases charitos, the God of all grace, will Himself katartizo, restore, His people.
basic.typology: The shepherd imagery runs from the Lord as Israel's Shepherd in Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 to Jesus the Good Shepherd, and now to elders as under-shepherds of the Chief Shepherd. The crown of glory answers the fading crowns of this world. And God's mighty hand recalls the hand that delivered Israel from Egypt, now lifting the humble in due time.
basic.christ: Christ is the Chief Shepherd, the owner of the flock and the coming Judge and rewarder of faithful shepherds. He is the one whose sufferings Peter witnessed and whose glory will be revealed. It is in Him that God has called His people to eternal glory. The whole passage is oriented to His appearing, when the unfading crown is given.
basic.god: God is the one who opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, whose mighty hand humbles and exalts in due time, and who cares personally for His people so that they can cast all their cares on Him. Above all He is the God of all grace who, after a little suffering, will Himself restore, secure, strengthen, and establish His own. He is gracious, caring, mighty, and faithful to the end.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 contrasts false shepherds with God the true Shepherd. John 21 records Jesus charging Peter to feed His sheep. Proverbs 3 and James 4 say God gives grace to the humble. And Psalm 55 says cast your burden on the Lord, and He will sustain you.
basic.oneStory: God has always shepherded His people, raising under-shepherds and finally coming Himself in Christ, the Good and Chief Shepherd. The suffering church is His flock, kept through a little while of affliction toward eternal glory. Humbling themselves, casting their cares on Him, and resisting the enemy, believers rest in the God of all grace, who will Himself restore them and bring them home, to whom belongs the power forever.

context.literary:
The paragraph is built as three nested movements, each ending on a pledge that looks forward. Verses 1 to 4 address one group, the elders, and close on a future event, the appearing of the Chief Shepherd. Verses 5 to 7 widen to the whole congregation and close on a present certainty, 'He cares for you.' Verses 8 to 11 turn outward to the enemy and close on a promise and a doxology. Each section pairs a duty with a reason, and in each the reason is God's own action.

The commands come in tidy contrasts. Verses 2 and 3 set three negatives against three positives, compulsion against willingness, greed against eagerness, domination against example. The same shape, 'not this, but that,' is how Peter taught slaves, wives and sufferers earlier in the letter, so the elders are being given the same ethic as everyone else. Verses 5 to 7 then run on a single thread of humility: submit, clothe yourselves, humble yourselves, cast. Verse 7 is grammatically attached to verse 6, so casting anxiety is the way humbling is carried out and not a separate topic.

Verses 8 and 9 are staccato. Two short imperatives, be sober-minded and be alert, then a description of the enemy, then two more, resist and stand firm. Verse 10 breaks the rhythm with a long sentence in which four future verbs are stacked on one subject, God, and the word 'Himself' leans on all four.

The section also closes the letter's own frame. The opening called the readers elect exiles, 1 Peter 1:1, and spoke of suffering 'for a little while,' 1 Peter 1:6. Here the little while ends, 'after you have suffered for a little while,' and the God who chose them finishes what He began. The 'revealed' glory of verse 1 and the 'appears' of verse 4 echo the revelation of Christ in 1 Peter 1:7 and 1:13.
context.historical:
Peter's readers lived in the provinces of what is now northern Turkey, 1 Peter 1:1, in small house churches that were new and exposed. They were led by elders, presbyteroi, a word borrowed from the synagogue and from the councils of any ancient town, where age and standing earned a hearing. In the churches the word shared its work with 'overseer,' and Acts 20:17 and 20:28 show one group called both, with the same shepherding job. Titus 1:5 and 1:7 do the same. So Peter is not speaking to a separate office from the one Paul names; he is speaking to the ordinary board of local leaders.

Money was a real danger. Teachers and officials in the Greco-Roman world were commonly paid, and Paul had to defend his refusal of pay, 1 Corinthians 9:12. Titus 1:7 and 1 Timothy 3:3 list freedom from the love of money as a mark of an overseer. 'Lording it over' was a danger of another kind, since the surrounding world assumed that a leader's role was to command, which is exactly what Jesus said, Mark 10:42-43.

The 'fiery trial' of 1 Peter 4:12 and the slander the readers faced, 1 Peter 2:12, 3:16, were social pressures more than organised state terror at this stage, though the letter knows the name 'Christian' could land a person before a governor, 4:16. Nothing in the text demands a date of formal empire wide persecution. Peter reminds them that 'your brothers throughout the world' share the same sufferings, 5:9, which would have been real news to isolated congregations that believed themselves alone.

The lion needs no explaining to hearers raised on the Psalms, where lions stand for violent enemies, Psalm 22:13, and to a Roman world in which the arena was a feature of life. Peter reaches for that picture to name something his readers already feared.
context.canonical:
Shepherding is one of the Bible's oldest pictures of leadership. Moses was tending a flock when he met God at the bush, Exodus 3:1, and David was lifted from the sheepfold to be shepherd of Israel, Psalm 78:70-72. When the kings failed, the prophets turned the image into an indictment. Ezekiel 34:2-4 condemns shepherds who feed themselves, ruling 'with violence and cruelty,' and Jeremiah 23:1-4 does the same, and in both God answers that He will search for the flock Himself and then set a faithful shepherd over it, Ezekiel 34:11 and 34:23. Peter's three negatives in verses 2 and 3 read like a point by point reversal of Ezekiel's charge sheet.

The New Testament then fills the picture. Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11, and the great Shepherd who was brought back from the dead, Hebrews 13:20. Peter himself was recommissioned on a beach with the words 'Feed My lambs' and 'Shepherd My sheep,' John 21:15-17. Earlier in this same letter he has called Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls,' 1 Peter 2:25. Paul's charge to the Ephesian elders, Acts 20:28, is the closest parallel, a flock bought at great price and watched over by those the Spirit has appointed.

The quotation in verse 5 comes from Proverbs 3:34 and is used again in James 4:6, so Peter and James draw on one well known proverb. The advice to cast cares on God leans on Psalm 55:22, and the warning about the devil sits beside James 4:7 and Ephesians 6:11-13. The promise of verse 10 is gathered up in Paul's prayers in 1 Thessalonians 5:23-24 and in Jude 24, where God is the one who keeps and presents His people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wants elders to hear this charge as the word of a man who has been where they are. He does not pull rank; he calls himself a fellow elder, and he mentions his own part in Christ's sufferings and his own share in coming glory. That is not decoration. Peter was the disciple who slept in the garden, Mark 14:37, who denied his Lord, and who was then told to feed His sheep, John 21:15-17. He is writing as a restored shepherd, and the shape of his advice, willingly, not for gain, not as a boss, comes from knowing what failure in each of those directions costs.

He also wants the whole congregation to see that leadership is held in place by something larger than the leaders. The flock is God's, the Chief Shepherd will come, the crown is His to give, so no elder is master and no member is merely a customer. That is why the words to the young and to everyone in verse 5 come straight after the charge to the elders: authority works only where humility runs both ways.

The turn to anxiety and the devil is aimed at weary people. Peter is not adding a new topic; he is naming what the pressure of the letter does to a believer, worry first, then a hungry enemy, then the temptation to think nobody else is suffering. His point is that the answer to each is the same, to cast, to resist, to stand with the worldwide family, and then to wait for the God who finishes the work.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this passage is direct instruction, and it does apply as it stands: shepherd willingly, do not use the work for gain, do not boss, set an example, be humble, cast your cares, stay alert, resist. The notes about elders are written to a particular group in a particular church setting, so how a congregation appoints, pays or structures its leaders is worked out from the whole of the New Testament, not from these verses alone.

Some lines describe rather than command. 'Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion' says what the enemy is like; it does not tell us to hunt him or to see him behind every difficulty. Peter's own reaction is to tell us to be sober and to resist, not to be sensational. Verse 9 states that believers worldwide suffer in the same way; that is a fact to be comforted by, not a rule that every Christian must expect the same trial.

The promises in verses 4 and 10 are given to the church as a whole under God's hand, and they are not a formula that the exact outcome of any one trial is guaranteed in this life. 'In due time' and 'a little while' are God's measure, not ours. Peter shows us the pattern of God's care without promising a timetable.

debates.question: Is the lion of verse 8 a picture of the devil's real activity, or of persecution?

views.label: A personal enemy who attacks believers
views.case: Peter names him: your adversary, antidikos, the devil, diabolos, the slanderer. The Bible shows him acting as accuser and tempter, Job 2:4-6, Zechariah 3:1, Luke 22:31, and the same letter grounds suffering in God's will, not in chance. Jesus' promise in Luke 22:31-32 shows Peter had learned firsthand that the enemy asks for people and that Christ prays.

views.label: The pressure of persecution, personified
views.case: Some stress the lion as an image of the state and the crowd that harassed the churches, and point to the lion's mouth in Psalm 22:13 and 2 Timothy 4:17. On this view the word 'devil' tells believers who stands behind the human opposition, but the verse is chiefly a warning about hostility they could see.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. The text uses the personal name, so the enemy is real, but he works through slander, fear and suffering, so the practical cure is the same either way, steady, faith filled resistance and the company of other believers, and the confidence that he is leashed, Job 1:12.

debates.question: Does the 'crown of glory' mean a special reward for elders, or the common hope of all believers?

views.label: A particular reward for faithful shepherds
views.case: The promise is made in the middle of a charge to elders, verses 1 to 4, and the language of a crown for faithful service matches 2 Timothy 4:8 and James 1:12. It is natural to take it as a reward for those who tended the flock as asked.

views.label: The shared hope of every believer
views.case: Peter's 'glory' language elsewhere belongs to the whole church, 1 Peter 1:7 and 5:10, and the elders are described as 'partakers of the glory to be revealed,' verse 1, a share open to everyone. Paul says the crown awaits 'all who crave His appearing,' 2 Timothy 4:8.

debates.bearing: Elders will give an account, Hebrews 13:17, so the promise has a particular weight for them. Even so, it is the Chief Shepherd's gift, not wages, and it never fades, so the passage presses elders to serve from the joy of the same grace they are urging on others.

debates.question: Is 'young men' in verse 5 a statement about age or about role?

views.label: Younger members of the church
views.case: The word neoteroi is a plain comparative, younger ones. It is set beside 'elders,' presbyteroi, a comparative form of 'old,' so Peter is pairing old and young in the way a household or village would. Acts 5:6 uses the same word for the young men who carried out Ananias.

views.label: Everyone not yet in leadership
views.case: Some think the word is broader than age, naming those who are subject to the elders. Peter's 'in the same way' echoes his earlier call to submit in 1 Peter 2:13 to 3:7, which spanned citizens, slaves and wives.

debates.bearing: Whichever the lean, the instruction rests on one principle. Authority in the church is received humbly and honoured humbly, and verse 5 turns at once to 'all of you' because mutual humility is the real command.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verb of the charge is a command to shepherd, and Peter adds participles that fill it out. 'Watching over,' episkopountes in verse 2, comes from the word behind 'overseer' and so ties the elders' work to the overseeing role in Acts 20:28; a few early manuscripts leave the participle out, so some translations omit it. Then come the three pairs. 'Compulsion' is anankastos, doing a thing because you are forced to. 'Greed' is aischrokerdos, literally shameful gain, the same family as the 'greedy for money' of Titus 1:7. And 'lording it over' is katakyrieuo, the same verb Jesus used of the rulers of the Gentiles in Mark 10:42, with its added prefix of downward domination. The positive 'examples' is typos, the mark left by a blow, then a mould or pattern, the word Paul uses in Philippians 3:17 and 1 Timothy 4:12. Elders are meant to stamp their own lives as the pattern the flock can copy.

The 'Chief Shepherd' of verse 4 is archipoimen, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The reward is a stephanos, the wreath given to a victor or honoured citizen, which is not the royal diadema. The 'unfading' of the crown is amarantinos, from the amaranth, a flower that was thought not to wither; it rhymes with the 'unfading' inheritance of 1 Peter 1:4, so the hope of the letter's opening comes back at its close.

In verse 5, 'clothe yourselves' is enkombosasthe, a rare verb drawn from a word for tying on a garment, often taken to mean the apron a slave fastened on before serving; the picture is of humility worn as work clothes. 'Opposes' is antitassetai, a military term for setting yourself in battle array against someone, and the quotation follows Proverbs 3:34 as it stands in the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew, as the BSB renders it, says God 'mocks the mockers.'

Verse 7 contains an aorist participle, epiripsantes, 'having cast,' which depends on the command 'humble yourselves' in verse 6. The verb means to throw something onto something else, as when the disciples threw their cloaks over the colt in Luke 19:35, and it picks up the Greek of Psalm 55:22. The reason clause 'He cares' uses melei, a verb of concern that Jesus used in the negative of the hired hand, 'unconcerned for the sheep,' John 10:13. The hired man is exactly the one who does not care; God, the owner, does.

In verse 8 the two commands nepsate and gregoresate, 'be sober' and 'be alert,' are the pair used in 1 Thessalonians 5:6, and gregoreo is what Jesus asked of Peter in Gethsemane, Mark 14:37-38. The enemy is antidikos, a legal opponent in a court case, as in Matthew 5:25 and Luke 12:58, and diabolos, the slanderer. 'Devour' is katapino, to swallow down, the word used for death 'swallowed up in victory,' 1 Corinthians 15:54. 'Resist' is anthistemi, the same verb James pairs with the devil's fleeing, James 4:7.

Verse 10 stacks four future indicatives, katartisei, sterixei, sthenosei, themeliosei, on 'Himself' in the emphatic position. Katartizo is used for mending nets, Matthew 4:21, and for restoring a fallen brother, Galatians 6:1; sterizo is what Jesus told Peter to do for his brothers, Luke 22:32; themelioo is to lay a foundation, as the wise builder did on rock, Matthew 7:25. Peter's own commission in Luke 22:32 comes back as God's promise to all.

typology.type: The shepherd king, from Moses and David to the Chief Shepherd
typology.fulfillment: Moses was called from his father in law's flock, Exodus 3:1, and David was taken from the sheepfold to shepherd God's people, Psalm 78:70-72. Both were under-shepherds of the Lord, who 'tends His flock like a shepherd,' Isaiah 40:11. Ezekiel promised that God would appoint 'one shepherd, My servant David,' Ezekiel 34:23, and Jesus claims the role, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11. Peter makes the escalation explicit with the title Chief Shepherd. The type falls short in that every earlier shepherd needed a flock he did not own and finally died; Christ owns the sheep and lays down His life for them and takes it up again, Hebrews 13:20.

typology.type: God's mighty hand, from the exodus to the humbled and exalted
typology.fulfillment: The phrase 'mighty hand' belongs to the exodus: the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt 'with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm,' Deuteronomy 5:15, and the same hand drove Pharaoh to let the people go, Exodus 6:1. Peter takes that hand and applies it to the church's trials. The hand that crushed Egypt is the hand under which believers bow, and the hand that will lift them in due time. The escalation is that the redemption is no longer from Pharaoh but from sin and death through the cross, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The type falls short in that Israel's deliverance was national and temporary, while this exaltation is 'to His eternal glory in Christ,' verse 10.

typology.type: The little while of exile, from Isaiah 54 to the church's suffering
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah told the exiles, 'For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back,' Isaiah 54:7. The pattern is a short darkness followed by a gathering. Peter's 'after you have suffered for a little while' belongs to the same grammar, and the letter has already called its readers exiles, 1 Peter 1:1 and 2:11. The correspondence rests on shared theme and shared shape and Peter does not cite Isaiah here, so it is an echo and not a declared fulfilment. The escalation is that the return is not to a land but to glory, and that the one who guarantees it, Christ, entered glory by way of the same suffering, 1 Peter 1:11.

typology.type: The victor's crown, from the Lord as a diadem to the unfading wreath
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 28:5 promises that 'the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people.' The honour the faithful receive is a share of God's own glory. Paul speaks of a perishable wreath won in the games against an imperishable one, 1 Corinthians 9:25, and of the crown of righteousness for all who long for Christ's appearing, 2 Timothy 4:8. Peter's version is the crown of glory that never fades. The type is imperfect because earthly crowns wither and go to one winner; this one is given to many and never dims.

study.christ:
The passage is leaning toward a person, and he is named by a title Peter coins: the Chief Shepherd. Every shepherd in the Bible, Moses, David, the elders of Israel, the leaders of the churches, works under a Shepherd who is greater. Verse 4 says that He will 'appear,' the word that belongs to His coming in glory, and that when He does He will give the crown. The elders are not the answer to the church's needs; they are placeholders for Him.

The Old Testament had already promised this shepherd. After condemning faithless leaders, Ezekiel 34:11 says 'I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out,' and then, in verse 23, God promises 'one shepherd, My servant David.' The same chapter first says God Himself will do the work and then says a servant of David will do it, which looks like two promises and turns out to be one. In Jesus the Lord comes to seek and the son of David feeds His people. John 10:11 and 10:14 show Him claiming the title. Hebrews 13:20 calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' raised from the dead. Revelation 7:17 pictures the Lamb as the shepherd who leads His people to living water.

Peter has taught in this letter that Christ's pattern in suffering is the pattern for His people. He 'suffered for you, leaving you an example,' 1 Peter 2:21, and 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 2:24, so that the straying sheep might return to 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls,' 2:25. The elders of 5:1 to 4 are asked to shepherd in that light. A shepherd who lords it over the flock denies the Chief Shepherd's own way. The one who 'did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, is the model, and the contrast with the hired hand who abandons the flock, John 10:12-13, is exactly what Peter's 'not for greed' protects.

Christ is also the explanation of why suffering can be called 'a little while.' He is the one who suffered and then entered glory; Peter, as a witness of the first and a partaker in the second, speaks from inside the pattern. When he says that God has called His people 'to His eternal glory in Christ,' verse 10, the phrase 'in Christ' is not filler. It is the sphere in which a suffering people already belong to the glory that will be revealed. Christ also stands behind the promise of verse 10, since Peter's own commission to 'strengthen your brothers,' Luke 22:32, came from the One who prayed for his faith. The Chief Shepherd keeps his own under-shepherds.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Not every detail in the passage is a coded picture of Jesus, and the lion is not a type of anything. What the text gives is the title, the appearing, the crown, and the pattern of humility, and the New Testament's use of the shepherd theme supplies the rest.
study.god:
The God of this passage is first of all a God who is above and near. He is the one under whose 'mighty hand' believers are to bow, verse 6, and the one who 'cares for you,' verse 7. Peter does not let either truth swallow the other. The hand that rules history is the hand that lifts the lowly, and the greatness that humbles proud people is the same greatness that carries a worried one. The Greek word for 'power' in the closing doxology, kratos, comes from the same family as the 'mighty' of verse 6, so the doxology says in praise what verse 6 says in submission.

He is a God who opposes the proud. The proverb quoted in verse 5 is blunt: He sets Himself against them, in the stance of a soldier against an enemy. Humility is therefore not a pleasant virtue but a matter of whose side we stand on, and the elder who bullies his flock is, whatever else he thinks, on the wrong side of that line. At the same time He 'gives grace to the humble.' This is the pattern of Isaiah 57:15, where the high and holy God 'inhabits eternity' and also dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit.'

He is a God who cares in particulars. The word 'anxiety' in verse 7 means the divided, pulled apart worry of life, and the invitation is to throw the whole of it, 'all your anxiety,' on Him. Jesus teaches the same in Matthew 6:25-34, with the same ground, that the heavenly Father knows. The care is not sentiment. It is the care of an owner who has paid for the flock, Acts 20:28, and who will not run when the wolf comes, John 10:12-13.

He permits an enemy and sets limits on him. Peter does not say that the devil is a rival god. He is an 'adversary,' and he prowls, and he can be resisted; God has the last word, as in Job 1:12 and 2:6, where the enemy can act only as far as he is let. The suffering of verse 9 is real and the enemy is real, and yet verse 10 puts all the active verbs in the mouth of God. The God of Peter's letter does not merely wait out suffering; He ends it, and He does so Himself.

He is the God of all grace, and the title is the heart of the passage. He is the source of every kind of grace, the grace that forgives, that sustains, and that finishes. His call was 'to His eternal glory in Christ,' which means the destination was fixed before the trial began. The four promises of verse 10 make a single movement: He repairs what is broken, fastens what is loose, fills what is weak and lays a foundation under what is shaken.

For worship, this means that humility, prayer and watchfulness are not our contribution to a bargain. They are the posture of people who rely on a God who has already promised to restore, and who gives Himself the glory and the power forever, verse 11.

crossReferences.note: God's indictment of Israel's shepherds, who fed themselves, did not strengthen the weak or search for the lost, and ruled 'with violence and cruelty.' Peter's three negatives, no compulsion, no greed, no lording it over, read as the reversal of this charge, and the promise that God would search for His flock Himself, Ezekiel 34:11, stands behind the Chief Shepherd.

Jesus restores Peter after the denial with the words 'Feed My lambs' and 'Shepherd My sheep.' The verb Peter now gives the elders is the verb he was given on the beach. His charge to others is a commission he received as a forgiven failure, which is why he writes without any air of superiority.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders to watch over the flock and 'be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.' The elders there are appointed by the Spirit and called overseers, so the verse shows that elder, overseer and shepherd describe one work. It also anchors Peter's 'God's flock' in the price Christ paid.

Jesus says the rulers of the Gentiles 'lord it over' their people, 'but it shall not be this way among you,' because the Son of Man came to serve and give His life. Peter uses the same verb for what elders must not do. The command in 1 Peter 5:3 is a standing application of a saying he heard from the Lord.

James quotes Proverbs 3:34 in the same words and builds on it a call to submit to God, resist the devil, and humble yourselves so that He will exalt you. The close match of the two letters shows a shared early Christian teaching, and James adds that resisting the devil leads to his fleeing.

David, betrayed by a close friend, tells himself to hand his load to the LORD, who holds up those who do and never lets the righteous be shaken. Peter's verb in verse 7 follows the Greek of this verse. The psalm supplies both the invitation and the promise, steadiness, which sits easily beside the 'establish you' of verse 10.

Jesus tells the crowd not to worry about food or clothing, because the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows what they need. Peter condenses the lesson into one line, because He cares for you. The same logic runs in both: anxiety is answered not by willpower but by the character of the Father.

Jesus warns Simon that Satan has asked to sift the disciples like wheat, and says He has prayed that Peter's faith will not fail and that when he has turned back he must strengthen his brothers. Peter's verse 8 warning is written from experience, and his word 'strengthen' in verse 10 is the verb of this commission, now promised by God to all.

Paul tells the church to be strong in the Lord, put on God's armour and stand against the devil's schemes, since the struggle is against spiritual powers and not flesh and blood. Both writers call for firm standing, and both place the strength in God, not in the believer.

'The God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep.' Where Peter looks ahead to the Chief Shepherd's appearing, Hebrews looks back to His resurrection. The one who comes is the one who died and was raised.

The opening of the letter promises a living hope and an imperishable, unfading inheritance reserved in heaven, and speaks of grief for a little while that proves faith more precious than gold. Chapter 5 returns to the same ground, the little while of suffering, the unfading crown, and the glory revealed, so that the letter ends where it began.

Paul prays that the God of peace Himself will sanctify them completely and keep them blameless, and adds, 'The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it.' It is the same ground as verse 10, that the God who calls is the God who completes, and He does it Himself.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world meant to be tended, Genesis 1:28 and 2:15, and a God who walks with His people. After the fall that care passes into a promise, and the picture the Bible chooses most often for it is a shepherd. Abraham and his sons are shepherds, Moses is a shepherd, and God Himself is called the Shepherd of Israel from Jacob's blessing onward, Genesis 48:15. When David is chosen, the shepherd becomes a king, Psalm 78:70-72, and Israel's hope is bound up with a shepherd king.

The story then turns dark. The leaders fail, the flock is scattered, and the exile is described as a flock driven from its pasture, Ezekiel 34:5-6 and Jeremiah 23:1-2. God's reply in Ezekiel 34:11 and Jeremiah 23:3 is that He will gather them, and that He will appoint a shepherd who will be faithful. The rest of the Old Testament waits for that shepherd, Micah 5:4.

Jesus enters the story as the answer, the good shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11, whom the prophet had seen struck so that the sheep would scatter, Zechariah 13:7, and who rose again as the great Shepherd, Hebrews 13:20. The church that Peter writes to is that flock gathered from Israel and the nations, one flock under one shepherd, John 10:16. Its elders are the first human shepherds of the new age, not a new priesthood but a ministry of care that points beyond itself.

Peter also places his readers in the long story of exile. They are scattered, harassed and hurried, and the enemy who first deceived humanity in a garden now prowls the world, Genesis 3:1 and Revelation 12:9. The answer he gives them is the old answer, to humble themselves under God's hand and to wait for His exaltation. What the exile cost, God will restore.

The story ends where verse 4 points. When the Chief Shepherd appears, the crown is given, and the Lamb shepherds His people to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17. The roaring lion is thrown down, Revelation 12:9-10 and 20:10. The suffering of 'a little while' passes, and the God of all grace brings His people into the glory He called them to, where there is no more death or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and the throne of God and of the Lamb is among them, Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: How are elders to shepherd God's flock?

options.text: Willingly and eagerly, not for gain, and not lording it over the flock but as examples.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3: humble, willing, exemplary care, not domination or greed.

options.text: By exercising firm control so the people obey.
options.note: Peter forbids lording it over those entrusted to them.

options.text: Only if they are paid well for their trouble.
options.note: They are to serve not out of greed but eagerly.

options.text: By leading through humble example rather than compulsion.
options.note: True and close, though the answer should include willingly and not for gain.

quiz.q: What will faithful elders receive when the Chief Shepherd appears?

options.text: The crown of glory that will never fade away.
options.note: Verse 4: an unfading crown from Christ the Chief Shepherd.

options.text: Public honor and status in this life.
options.note: The reward is an eternal, unfading crown, not present status.

options.text: Nothing; faithful service is its own reward alone.
options.note: Peter promises a real reward at Christ's appearing.

options.text: An eternal reward given by Christ Himself.
options.note: True, though the answer should name the unfading crown of glory.

quiz.q: Why are believers to clothe themselves with humility?

options.text: Because God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
options.note: Verse 5: humility is the posture God blesses with grace.

options.text: Because humility makes people like them more.
options.note: The reason given is God's response to humility, not human approval.

options.text: Because they have nothing worth being proud of.
options.note: The ground is God's grace to the humble, not mere self-deprecation.

options.text: So that under God's mighty hand He may exalt them in due time.
options.note: True, verse 6, though the stated reason is that God gives grace to the humble.

quiz.q: How are believers to handle their anxieties?

options.text: Cast them all on God, because He cares for them.
options.note: Verse 7: throw the whole burden on God, grounded in His personal care.

options.text: Carry them privately so as not to burden God.
options.note: Peter says to cast them on God, who cares for you.

options.text: Ignore them and hope they pass.
options.note: The call is to entrust cares to God, not to ignore them.

options.text: Entrust every worry to the God who cares for them.
options.note: True to the sense, though the answer should stress casting them all on Him.

quiz.q: What does Peter promise from the God of all grace after a little suffering?

options.text: That God Himself will restore, secure, strengthen, and establish His people.
options.note: Verse 10: the letter's summit promise of God mending His suffering people.

options.text: That believers will be spared all further hardship at once.
options.note: The suffering is for a little while first; then God restores.

options.text: That the strong will make themselves secure.
options.note: It is God who Himself restores and establishes, not human strength.

options.text: That God will bring His people through suffering to eternal glory.
options.note: True to the sense, though the answer should name that God Himself restores and establishes them.

questions: Peter charges shepherds to lead humbly by example, not by domination. Wherever you have influence over others, how does this reshape the way you lead?
God gives grace to the humble but opposes the proud. Where is pride quietly at work in you, and what would it look like to clothe yourself in humility instead?
Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. What specific worry will you hand to God today, trusting that He genuinely cares?
The devil prowls like a roaring lion, yet is to be resisted by faith. What lies or pressures are you facing, and how does standing firm in faith answer them?
The God of all grace promises to restore you after a little suffering. How does knowing your suffering is brief and your glory eternal steady you right now?

translationNotes.note: Be shepherds renders poimaino, to tend a flock; some manuscripts omit watching over them, but the sense of oversight remains in the surrounding phrases.
God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble quotes Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, also cited in James 4:6.
Restore translates katartizo, to mend or make complete, used of setting bones or repairing nets; some manuscripts add in Christ Jesus to called you to His eternal glory.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 1 Peter 5:1-11.
